title: ARCANE: Adaptive RISC-V Cache Architecture for Near-memory Extensions
problem: Von Neumann architectures suffer from data movement bottlenecks (extensive memory traffic, low throughput, poor energy efficiency). Existing accelerators improve performance but lack flexibility and require explicit data transfers; compute in-/near-memory solutions face usability challenges due to data placement constraints.
motivation: Modern data-driven applications (CNNs, analytics) are memory-bound; near-memory compute addresses energy efficiency but software burden of explicit data placement limits adoption.
method: ARCANE puts a computing unit directly inside the cache memory—the fast storage between your CPU and main memory. A RISC-V controller (a processor using a standard instruction set) takes custom instructions from the main CPU and runs vector operations (calculations on multiple data items at once) on data already stored in cache. Because computation happens where data sits, instead of moving data back and forth to a distant processor, most data stays fast. The architecture automatically handles data placement and synchronization, so programmers never need to manually move data around.
key_novelty: Computing moves into the cache using RISC-V instructions, with automatic data placement eliminating manual data movement.
contributions: RISC-V cache controller with near-memory vector processing for CNN workloads
30-84x performance improvement on 8-bit data vs. traditional cache + CPU
Automatic data placement abstraction reducing software burden; 41.3% area overhead for worst-case 32-bit workloads
limitations: Evaluation on CNN workloads; generalization to other memory-bound workloads and scalability to multi-core systems not discussed.
primary_theme: cache-integrated near-memory computing with ISA abstraction
